transcript.heading: News Report One (British Male)
paras: Luxembourg made history in March by becoming the first country in the world to make all public transport completely free. The policy applies to every person in the country, as well as cross-border workers commuting from neighboring Belgium, France, and Germany. Before this change, fares had already been very low, costing about two euros for a day pass, but the government decided to abolish all tickets entirely. Officials hope that removing fares entirely will encourage more people to leave their cars at home. Luxembourg has some of the worst traffic congestion in Europe, with hundreds of thousands of cross-border workers driving in daily from surrounding countries. The capital city, Luxembourg City, has only about 110,000 residents but sees enormous traffic jams during rush hour as over 400,000 workers enter the country each day. The government has also been investing in expanding train and bus services to make public transport a more convenient option. While the policy costs the government about 41 million euros annually in lost ticket revenue, supporters argue that the economic benefits from reduced traffic and lower pollution will outweigh the costs.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.
1. What major policy did Luxembourg implement in March?
2. What is the main goal of this new transport policy?

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Male)
paras: Libraries across Canada have introduced an unusual program to help children improve their reading skills: reading to dogs. The "Paws for Stories" initiative brings specially trained therapy dogs into local libraries, where children can sit and read aloud to the calm, friendly animals. The dogs are certified through national therapy animal organizations and have undergone extensive training to remain calm and gentle in all situations. Librarians report that many children feel anxious or self-conscious reading aloud in front of teachers or peers, fearing they will be judged for making mistakes. However, when reading to a dog, that anxiety disappears because the animal provides a non-judgmental, comforting presence. Children can read at their own pace, stumble over words without embarrassment, and gain confidence in their abilities. Studies from several school boards have shown measurable improvements in participating children's vocabulary, reading fluency, and overall confidence after just eight weeks in the program. Many libraries report waiting lists for the program, and similar initiatives have now spread to parts of the United States and the United Kingdom.
Questions 3 to 5 are based on the news report you have just heard.
3. Where have "reading with dogs" programs become popular?
4. What kind of dogs participate in this program?
5. What is the main reason children feel comfortable reading to dogs?

transcript.heading: News Report Three (British Male)
paras: An Indian entrepreneur has developed a creative solution to the global plastic waste problem: edible cutlery. Narayana Peesapaty, the founder of Bakeys, started producing spoons, forks, and chopsticks made entirely from sorghum, rice, and wheat flour. The utensils come in several flavors, including plain, sugar, ginger-cinnamon, and cumin, and are completely safe to eat. They have a shelf life of about three years and will naturally decompose within a week if discarded instead of eaten. Peesapaty got the idea when he realized that India alone throws away over 120 billion plastic utensils each year, most of which end up in landfills or waterways. Unlike biodegradable plastics that still require industrial composting facilities, Bakeys' products can either be eaten as a nutritious snack or simply thrown away where they will break down naturally. The company now sells over 1.5 million pieces of edible cutlery each month and exports to more than 15 countries. They have also expanded their product line to include edible cups and bowls, with plans to create edible packaging for other foods as well.
Questions 6 and 7 are based on the news report you have just heard.
6. What are Bakeys edible utensils made from?
7. How long does it take for discarded edible cutlery to decompose naturally?

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Sarah): Hey Mark, have you thought about what you want to do for volunteer work this semester? The student volunteer fair is this Thursday, and there are going to be dozens of organizations there.

Man (Mark): I've been meaning to look into that, Sarah, but I'm not sure where to start. I did some shelf stocking at the community food bank back home during high school, but I'd like to try something different now.

Woman: Oh, there's tons of options this year. The environmental club is organizing river and park cleanup days, there's a tutoring program for local elementary school kids, and the children's hospital is looking for people to help with activity nights. Oh, and there's a fun run this Saturday to raise money for the children's hospital too.
Man: Wait, that fun run this Saturday... is that the one in the morning?
Woman: Yeah, it starts at 8 AM, why?

Man: Oh no, that's my birthday! My parents are coming into town and they're throwing me a lunch party at that new Italian restaurant downtown. I completely forgot about that when I was thinking about volunteering.

Woman: That's okay, there are plenty of other events. The big river cleanup is the Saturday after next, from 9 AM to 1 PM. They provide gloves, garbage bags, snacks, and after we finish, there's a free barbecue lunch and party for all volunteers at the park pavilion.
Man: That sounds great, actually. I like being outside, and I've always cared about keeping our rivers clean. Do you know if we need any experience?

Woman: No experience necessary at all! They just ask that you wear closed-toe shoes and clothes you don't mind getting dirty. I did the cleanup last semester with some friends from my dorm, and it was actually really fun. We found some interesting things in the bushes - a bicycle, a perfectly good picnic basket, even a rubber chicken.
Man: That's hilarious. Alright, I'm definitely signing up for that. Do you want to go to the volunteer fair together on Thursday to sign up?
Woman: Sure thing! Let's meet outside the student union at 11 AM, right after my sociology class.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

9. What volunteer work has Mark done before?

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Emma): Hi David, it's Emma! I hope I'm not calling at a bad time.
Man (David): Hey Emma! Not at all, I was just making dinner. What's up?
Woman: Well, I have some exciting news - I finally found a new apartment! It's in that building complex by the park, with the gym and the rooftop garden.
Man: That's awesome! Congratulations! When are you moving?

Woman: The Saturday after next, on the 24th. That's why I'm calling, actually. I remember you have that pickup truck you use for your furniture projects, and I was wondering if I could borrow it? I'd completely fill up the gas tank and buy you dinner afterward, of course.

Man: Sure thing! The truck is available that day. Actually, I don't have anything planned that weekend, so I can help you move furniture too, if you want. It's easier with two people carrying couches and beds.
Woman: Really? That would be amazing! I was stressing about how I was going to get my bed frame and my bookshelf moved. I've already started packing, but I feel like I have so much stuff.

Man: Don't worry, everyone feels that way when they move. A word of advice, though - I have a whole stack of flattened moving boxes in my garage from when I moved last year. You can have those for free, that'll save you from buying them. Also, make sure you pack a separate suitcase with a change of clothes, your toothbrush, medications, and any important documents - things you'll need that first night when you're too tired to unpack boxes.
Woman: That's such a good idea. I remember last time I moved, I couldn't find my pajamas or my coffee maker for three days because everything was in unlabeled boxes.

Man: Oh right, and label every single box with which room it goes to, and mark boxes with fragile stuff clearly. Also, don't buy too much new furniture until after you move in - the building manager at my old place told me that when people move out, there's usually perfectly good furniture left behind, and they collect it in the basement to either donate or sell cheaply to new residents. I got a nice coffee table that way for 10 dollars.
Woman: That's a great tip! I was just about to buy a new dining set, I'll definitely wait and see what's available first.

13. When is Emma moving?

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Male)
paras: Walking is one of the simplest and most underrated forms of exercise, and recent research continues to confirm its remarkable health benefits. A 2023 study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association found that people who walked just 7,000 steps per day had a 50 percent lower risk of premature death compared to those who walked fewer than 3,000 steps daily. Contrary to popular belief, the study found that the famous 10,000 step goal isn't necessary for significant health benefits - the biggest reduction in mortality risk came from moving from a sedentary lifestyle to even moderate levels of walking. The benefits extended to all age groups, but were particularly pronounced in older adults. Walking also has significant mental health benefits; multiple studies have shown that a 30-minute walk can reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression as effectively as some medications for mild cases, without any side effects. Even small changes can make a big difference. "Active commuting," or walking or biking to work or school instead of driving, adds an average of 30 minutes of physical activity to people's daily routines without requiring them to set aside extra time for exercise. Japanese researchers have also done extensive studies on "forest bathing," or walking in natural environments, finding that it reduces cortisol, the stress hormone, significantly more effectively than walking in urban environments.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Female)
paras: Social media has become an inescapable part of modern life, with the average person spending about two and a half hours per day on social platforms. While these services offer obvious benefits - helping people stay connected with distant friends and family, providing access to information, and creating communities for people with shared interests - researchers are increasingly concerned about their negative impacts on mental health, particularly for teenagers. A 2024 Pew Research survey found that over 60 percent of teen girls reported that Instagram made them feel worse about their bodies and their lives, compared to just 20 percent who reported positive effects. The constant stream of carefully curated, filtered images of perfect vacations, perfect bodies, and perfect social lives creates an unrealistic standard that leaves many young people feeling inadequate. The phenomenon of "doomscrolling" - endlessly scrolling through negative news content - has also been linked to increased anxiety and feelings of helplessness. However, social media isn't entirely negative. During natural disasters and humanitarian crises, platforms have proven invaluable for organizing relief efforts and locating missing people, and viral fundraisers have raised over 100 million dollars for disaster relief in recent years. Experts suggest a balanced approach: setting daily time limits of 30 to 60 minutes for recreational social media use, being intentional about who you follow (unfollowing accounts that make you feel bad about yourself), and taking regular "digital detox" breaks.

19. What percentage of teen girls reported Instagram made them feel worse?
20. What is "doomscrolling"?
21. What positive impact of social media is mentioned?

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: Before the internet and big-box garden stores, mail-order seed catalogs were how millions of Americans got their garden seeds each spring. The business of selling seeds by mail began in the mid-1800s, but it truly exploded in popularity in the early 1900s, when companies began printing colorful, beautifully illustrated catalogs that arrived in mailboxes every January, right in the middle of winter when gardeners were eagerly planning their spring plantings. The most famous of these companies was W. Atlee Burpee & Company, founded by Washington Atlee Burpee in 1876. Burpee was different from other seed companies because he actually tested every seed variety he sold in multiple trial grounds across different climate zones, guaranteeing that seeds would germinate and grow true to type. Before Burpee, many seed companies sold poor-quality seeds that wouldn't grow, or seeds that were mislabeled. Burpee introduced many famous vegetable varieties that are still popular today, including Iceberg lettuce, Golden Bantam sweet corn, and the Big Boy tomato. Seed catalogs weren't just for ordering; they were a form of entertainment during long winter months, with families gathering around the kitchen table to look through the pages and decide which vegetables and flowers they would grow that year. Today, while many people buy seeds at local nurseries or online, mail-order seed catalogs still exist, and many gardeners look forward to receiving them each year as a beloved winter tradition.
Questions 23 to 25 are based on the passage you have just heard.
23. When did mail-order seed catalogs become extremely popular?
24. What made Burpee Seeds different from its competitors?
25. What did families often do with seed catalogs besides ordering seeds?
